questions.question: Which one of the following is non-crystalline or amorphous in nature?
questions.answer:
**(D)** Glass

**Glass** is an **amorphous (non-crystalline) solid** — a super-cooled liquid whose particles have no long-range order, so it has no sharp melting point and breaks with a conchoidal fracture. Diamond, graphite and common salt all give sharp X-ray diffraction patterns, i.e. their atoms/ions are arranged in a regular repeating lattice, so they are crystalline.

questions.question: An ionic compound has bcc structure with atoms A occupying the corners of the unit cell and B at the body centre. The formula of the ionic compound is
questions.answer:
**(A)** AB

Contribution of the corner atoms A:

$$8\times\tfrac18=1$$

Contribution of the body-centred atom B: $1$ (wholly inside the cell).

$$\ce{A : B}=1:1\ \Rightarrow\ \text{formula } \ce{AB}$$

So the compound is AB — the caesium-chloride type arrangement, in which each ion has coordination number 8.

questions.question: The molarity of the solution containing 5 g of NaOH in 500 ml of aqueous solution is
questions.answer:
**(C)** 0.25 M

Molar mass of NaOH $=23+16+1=40\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$:

$$n=\frac{5}{40}=0.125\ \text{mol}$$

$$M=\frac{n}{V}=\frac{0.125}{0.500}=0.25\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$$

**0.25 M.** Note that the volume is of the *solution*, not of the water — 5 g of NaOH in 500 mL of solution is what the question specifies.

questions.question: Relative lowering in vapour pressure is equal to
questions.answer:
**(C)** mole fraction of solute

Raoult's law for a solution of a non-volatile solute states

$$\frac{p^\circ-p_s}{p^\circ}=x_2=\frac{n_2}{n_1+n_2}$$

So the *relative* lowering of vapour pressure equals the **mole fraction of the solute** — this is one of the colligative properties, and it is the only one that needs no assumption about the solute's molar mass. The absolute lowering is $p^\circ x_2$.

questions.question: The charge required for the reduction of 1 mol of Al$^{3+}$ to Al is
questions.answer:
**(C)** 289500 C

$$\ce{Al^{3+} + 3e^- -> Al}$$

Three moles of electrons are needed per mole of aluminium, and one faraday is 96500 C:

$$Q=3\times96500=289500\ \text{C}$$

So 3 F (289500 C) gives 27 g of aluminium — this is the basis of the Hall–Héroult aluminium electrolysis.

questions.question: The unit of cell constant is
questions.answer:
**(D)** cm$^{-1}$

The cell constant is the ratio of the distance between the electrodes to their area:

$$G^*=\frac{l}{A}$$

Both $l$ and $A$ are lengths, so its unit is cm/cm$^2$ = **cm$^{-1}$** (or m$^{-1}$). It is related to the measured conductance by $\kappa=G\,G^*$, so conductivity has units S cm$^{-1}$ = ohm$^{-1}$ cm$^{-1}$.

questions.question: A reaction is first order in A and second order in B. How is the rate affected when concentrations of both A and B are doubled?
questions.answer:
**(C)** It increases 8 times

$$\text{rate}=k[\ce{A}][\ce{B}]^2$$

Doubling both:

$$\text{rate}'=k(2[\ce{A}])(2[\ce{B}])^2=8k[\ce{A}][\ce{B}]^2=8\,\text{rate}$$

The factor is $2^1\times2^2=2^3=8$ — the rate increases eight times, since the overall order is three.

questions.question: Molecularity of a reaction cannot be
questions.answer:
**(A)** 0

Molecularity is the number of species that collide simultaneously in an elementary step, so it must be a **whole number equal to or greater than one** — 1 (unimolecular), 2 (bimolecular), 3 (termolecular, rare). **Zero molecularity is meaningless**, since a reaction with no colliding species cannot occur. (Order, by contrast, *can* be zero, because it is an experimentally measured exponent.)

questions.question: Which of the following is aerosol?
questions.answer:
**(A)** Smoke

An **aerosol** is a colloid in which the dispersion medium is a **gas**. In smoke the dispersed phase is a solid (soot particles) in air — a solid aerosol. (Soap lather is a gas-in-liquid **foam**; milk is a liquid-in-liquid **emulsion**; butter is a liquid-in-solid emulsion/gel.)

questions.question: The process of settling of colloidal particles is called
questions.answer:
**(C)** coagulation

**Coagulation** (flocculation) is the **aggregation and settling** of colloidal particles, brought about by removing the charge that keeps them apart — by adding an electrolyte (Hardy–Schulze rule: the ion of opposite charge to the sol, with greater valency, is more effective), by heating, or by electrophoresis. Peptization is the reverse process; dialysis removes small ions; electrophoresis merely moves the particles.

questions.question: Calamine is an ore of
questions.answer:
**(A)** Zn

Calamine is **zinc carbonate, $\ce{ZnCO3}$** (the mineral hemimorphite is related). It is calcined to the oxide and then reduced with carbon:

$$\ce{ZnCO3 ->[\Delta] ZnO + CO2}$$

$$\ce{ZnO + C -> Zn + CO}$$

(Other zinc ores: zinc blende ZnS, zincite ZnO; bauxite is the ore of Al, haematite of Fe, copper pyrite of Cu.)

questions.question: Leaching is a process for
questions.answer:
**(B)** concentration

**Leaching** is the **chemical concentration of an ore** by dissolving it selectively in a suitable reagent, leaving the gangue behind. Examples: bauxite is leached with hot NaOH (Bayer's process) to give sodium aluminate, and gold/silver ores are leached with dilute NaCN:

$$\ce{4Au + 8NaCN + O2 + 2H2O -> 4Na[Au(CN)2] + 4NaOH}$$

Unlike physical methods, leaching is a chemical process, but its purpose is still concentration of the ore.

questions.question: Which of the following processes is used for purification of nickel?
questions.answer:
**(B)** Mond's process

Impure nickel is heated with **carbon monoxide at about 330 K**, giving volatile nickel tetracarbonyl, which is then decomposed at 450–470 K to give pure nickel:

$$\ce{Ni + 4CO ->[330\ K] Ni(CO)4 ^}$$

$$\ce{Ni(CO)4 ->[450-470\ K] Ni + 4CO}$$

The method works because only nickel forms a volatile carbonyl, so it separates nickel from cobalt and copper impurities. (Zone refining is for ultra-pure Si/Ge; Van Arkel for Ti/Zr; floatation is concentration, not refining.)

questions.question: Which of the following does not exist?
questions.answer:
**(B)** NCl$_5$

Nitrogen is a small atom with **no d orbitals available** in its valence shell, so it cannot expand its covalence beyond four — it can form NCl$_3$ but **not NCl$_5$**. Phosphorus, arsenic and antimony are larger and have vacant d orbitals, so PCl$_5$, AsCl$_5$ and SbCl$_5$ exist (and SbCl$_5$ is even a useful chlorinating agent / Lewis acid). This is the classic illustration of the absence of $d\pi$-$p\pi$ bonding in nitrogen.

questions.question: Process of commercial production of nitric acid is
questions.answer:
**(B)** Ostwald's process

In the **Ostwald process** ammonia is oxidised over a platinum–rhodium catalyst, and the NO so formed is oxidised to NO$_2$ and absorbed in water:

$$\ce{4NH3 + 5O2 ->[Pt][800 K] 4NO + 6H2O}$$

$$\ce{2NO + O2 -> 2NO2}$$

$$\ce{3NO2 + H2O -> 2HNO3 + NO}$$

(The Haber process makes ammonia; the contact process makes sulphuric acid; Deacon's process makes chlorine.)

questions.question: Which of the following acids is a tribasic acid?
questions.answer:
**(D)** H$_3$PO$_4$

Basicity is set by the number of **P–OH** groups (only H attached to oxygen is acidic):

- $\ce{H3PO4}$: $\ce{O=P(OH)3}$ — **three** P–OH → **tribasic**.
- $\ce{H3PO3}$: $\ce{O=P(H)(OH)2}$ — two P–OH → dibasic.
- $\ce{H3PO2}$: $\ce{H2P(O)(OH)}$ — one P–OH → monobasic.
- $\ce{HPO3}$ (metaphosphoric acid) is monobasic.

So only orthophosphoric acid, $\ce{H3PO4}$, is tribasic.

questions.question: Which one of the following is diamagnetic in nature?
questions.answer:
**(D)** Zn$^{2+}$

Zn$^{2+}$ is $3d^{10}$ — **all electrons paired**, so it has no unpaired electron and is **diamagnetic**. The others all have unpaired d electrons ($\ce{Co^{2+}}$: $3d^7$, three unpaired; $\ce{Ni^{2+}}$: $3d^8$, two unpaired; $\ce{Cu^{2+}}$: $3d^9$, one) and are therefore paramagnetic.

questions.question: Colours of transition metal ions are due to absorption of light of some wavelength. This results in
questions.answer:
**(A)** $d$–$d$ transition

In a complex the ligands split the five d orbitals into sets of different energy. When the ion has an **incompletely filled d subshell**, an electron can be promoted from the lower to the higher set by absorbing visible light; the light *not* absorbed is what we see, so the ion appears coloured. This is the **$d$–$d$ transition**, and it explains why $\ce{Cu^{2+}}$ ($d^9$) is blue and $\ce{Zn^{2+}}$ ($d^{10}$) is colourless. (Charge-transfer bands can also colour ions, e.g. permanganate.)

questions.question: Which of the following is ambidentate ligand?
questions.answer:
**(B)** CN$^-$

An **ambidentate ligand** has two different donor atoms and can attach through either. The cyanide ion can coordinate through **carbon** (as in $\ce{[Fe(CN)6]^{4-}}$) or through **nitrogen** (as in $\ce{[Fe(CN)5(NO)]^{2-}}$ or in Prussian blue), giving linkage isomers. Thiocyanate, $\ce{SCN^-}$ (S or N), and nitrite, $\ce{NO2^-}$ (N or O), are other examples. Hydroxide, water and sulphate have a single donor atom each (or are symmetric), so they are not ambidentate.

questions.question: CH$_3$CH$_2$Cl + NaI $\xrightarrow{\text{acetone}}$ CH$_3$CH$_2$I + NaCl. The reaction is
questions.answer:
**(B)** Finkelstein reaction

An alkyl chloride is refluxed with **NaI in dry acetone**; NaI is soluble in acetone while NaCl and NaBr are not, so the precipitation of NaCl drives the equilibrium to the iodide:

$$\ce{CH3CH2Cl + NaI ->[\text{acetone}] CH3CH2I + NaCl v}$$

It is an S$_N$2 substitution and the standard way of preparing alkyl iodides. (The reverse — iodide to chloride/bromide in acetone — is the Swarts reaction, which makes alkyl fluorides with AgF or Hg$_2$F$_2$.)

questions.question: Which of the following will react faster in S$_N$2 reaction?
questions.answer:
**(A)** 1-bromopropane

In an S$_N$2 reaction the nucleophile attacks the carbon from the side opposite the halogen, so **steric hindrance at the reaction centre decides the rate**. 1-Bromopropane is a **primary** halide — the least crowded — so it reacts fastest. 2-Bromopropane is secondary and therefore slower; 2-bromo-2-methylbutane is tertiary and reacts mainly by S$_N$1 (or eliminates). ('3-bromopropane' does not exist: a three-carbon chain has only C-1 and C-2.) The order is primary > secondary > tertiary, the reverse of S$_N$1.

questions.question: What is the IUPAC name of CH$_3$—O—C$_2$H$_5$?
questions.answer:
**(C)** Methoxyethane

The ether is $\ce{CH3-O-CH2CH3}$. The larger group (ethyl, two carbons) supplies the parent chain, and the smaller (methyl) becomes the alkoxy substituent:

$$\ce{CH3-O-C2H5}$$

So the name is **methoxyethane** (trivial name: ethyl methyl ether). Methoxymethane is $\ce{CH3OCH3}$; ethoxyethane is $\ce{C2H5OC2H5}$.

questions.question: Hydration of propene in the presence of dil. H$_2$SO$_4$ gives
questions.answer:
**(B)** CH$_3$—CH(OH)—CH$_3$

Acid-catalysed hydration of an unsymmetrical alkene follows **Markovnikov's rule**: the proton adds to the carbon bearing more hydrogens, so that the more stable (secondary) carbocation is formed, and water then attacks it:

$$\ce{CH3-CH=CH2 + H2O ->[H2SO4] CH3-CH(OH)-CH3}$$

The product is **propan-2-ol**, not propan-1-ol. (Anti-Markovnikov hydration, giving propan-1-ol, needs hydroboration–oxidation with $\ce{BH3/THF}$ then $\ce{H2O2/OH^-}$.)

questions.question: In Acetaldehyde + 4[H] $\xrightarrow{Zn-Hg/HCl}$ A, A is
questions.answer:
**(B)** Ethane

Zinc amalgam with concentrated hydrochloric acid (**Clemmensen reduction**) reduces the carbonyl group — even of an aldehyde — completely to a $\ce{-CH3}$ group:

$$\ce{CH3CHO + 4[H] ->[Zn-Hg/HCl] CH3-CH3 + H2O}$$

The product is **ethane**. The reagent operates in strong acid, so it is used for compounds that would not survive the alkaline Wolff–Kishner conditions.

questions.question: Tollens' reagent is
options: a solution of copper sulphate, sodium citrate and sodium carbonate
questions.answer:
**(B)** ammoniacal silver nitrate solution

**Tollens' reagent** is silver nitrate solution made alkaline with ammonia until the initial precipitate just redissolves, giving $[\ce{Ag(NH3)2}]^+$:

$$\ce{AgNO3 + NH4OH -> AgOH v ->[NH4OH] [Ag(NH3)2]^+ + OH^-}$$

Aldehydes reduce it to metallic silver, giving the **silver mirror**:

$$\ce{RCHO + 2[Ag(NH3)2]^+ + 3OH^- -> RCOO^- + 2Ag v + 4NH3 + 2H2O}$$

(Option (3) describes **Fehling's** solution, used similarly; option (4) is Lucas reagent.)

questions.question: In Benzaldehyde + [O] $\xrightarrow{\text{Air}}$ A, A is
questions.answer:
**(B)** Benzoic acid

Aldehydes are oxidised readily, even by atmospheric oxygen, to the carboxylic acid:

$$\ce{2C6H5CHO + O2 -> 2C6H5COOH}$$

This **autoxidation** goes through a peroxy-acid intermediate and explains why benzaldehyde (oil of bitter almonds) develops a white crystalline deposit of benzoic acid in an old, partly empty bottle. Benzyl alcohol would be a *reduction* product.

questions.question: When acetamide is heated with an aqueous solution of sodium hydroxide and bromine, the product formed is
questions.answer:
**(A)** Methylamine

The **Hofmann bromamide (Hofmann degradation)** removes the carbonyl group and gives a primary amine with **one carbon less**:

$$\ce{CH3CONH2 + Br2 + 4NaOH -> CH3NH2 + Na2CO3 + 2NaBr + 2H2O}$$

So acetamide (two carbons) gives **methylamine** (one carbon). The mechanism passes through N-bromoacetamide, which rearranges with migration of the methyl group to nitrogen, giving methyl isocyanate, then the amine.

questions.question: Which of the following is functional group of primary amine?
questions.answer:
**(B)** —NH$_2$

The amino group **$\ce{-NH2}$** is the functional group of a **primary** amine, $\ce{RNH2}$: the nitrogen bears two hydrogens and one alkyl/aryl group, and it has one lone pair. A secondary amine has $\ce{-NHR}$ (one H on N) and a tertiary amine $\ce{-NR2}$ (no H on N). '—NH$_3$' and '—NH$_4^+$' are not univalent groups; $\ce{-NH3^+}$ would be a protonated ammonium centre.

questions.question: Proteins are polymers of amino acids, that are connected to each other by
questions.answer:
**(C)** peptide bond

Amino acids are joined by the **peptide bond**, $\ce{-CO-NH-}$, formed between the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amino group of the next, with loss of water:

$$\ce{H2N-CH(R)-COOH + H2N-CH(R')-COOH -> H2N-CH(R)-CO-NH-CH(R')-COOH + H2O}$$

(Glycosidic bonds join sugars; phosphodiester bonds join nucleotides in nucleic acids.)

questions.question: Which base is not found in DNA?
questions.answer:
**(C)** Uracil (U)

DNA contains the purines **adenine and guanine** and the pyrimidines **cytosine and thymine**. **Uracil replaces thymine in RNA only** — so uracil is not a constituent of DNA. (The other difference is the sugar: 2-deoxy-D-ribose in DNA, D-ribose in RNA.)

questions.question: Rickets is caused due to deficiency of
questions.answer:
**(D)** Vitamin D

**Rickets** — soft, deformed, poorly mineralised bones in children, with bow legs and delayed closure of the fontanelles — is caused by a deficiency of **vitamin D** (calciferol). Vitamin D is needed for the absorption of calcium and phosphate and for their deposition in bone; deficiency gives low plasma calcium and unmineralised osteoid. (Vitamin A deficiency → night blindness; B → beri-beri/pellagra; C → scurvy.)

questions.question: Caprolactum is monomer of
questions.answer:
**(A)** Nylon 6

**Caprolactam** (6-aminohexanoic acid lactam, a seven-membered ring with an $\ce{-NH-CO-}$ group) undergoes **ring-opening polymerisation** with water to give **Nylon 6**:

$$\ce{n\ \text{caprolactam} + H2O -> [-NH-(CH2)5-CO-]_n}$$

Nylon 6,6 is made from **adipic acid and hexamethylenediamine**; bakelite from phenol and formaldehyde; terylene from ethylene glycol and terephthalic acid.

questions.question: The element which is added to raw rubber to improve its physical properties is
questions.answer:
**(B)** Sulphur

**Vulcanisation** — heating raw rubber with **sulphur** (2–5%) — introduces sulphur bridges ($\ce{-C-S-C-}$) between the long polyisoprene chains. The cross-links stop the chains sliding over one another, so the rubber becomes stronger, harder, more elastic, and resistant to heat, oxidation and solvents. Without it, natural rubber is soft and tacky when warm and brittle when cold.

questions.question: Which of the following is used as disinfectant?
questions.answer:
**(B)** 0·2% phenol

Phenol is used as an **antiseptic** in low concentration (0.2–1%) and as a **disinfectant** for instruments, floors and excreta in stronger solution; it was the first surgical antiseptic (Lister). (Soframycin is an antibiotic, equanil (meprobamate) a tranquilliser, morphine a narcotic analgesic.)

questions.question: Barbituric acid is an example of
questions.answer:
**(A)** Tranquilizer

Barbituric acid is the parent of the **barbiturates** (veronal, luminal, seconal), which are central-nervous-system depressants used as **tranquillisers, sedatives and hypnotics**. Their derivatives depress the CNS and induce sleep; an overdose causes respiratory failure, which is why they have largely been replaced by the benzodiazepines. (Barbiturates are not antibiotics, analgesics or antacids.)

questions.question: What is the unit of first order rate constant?
questions.answer:
The unit is **s$^{-1}$ (per second)**.

For a first-order reaction, $\text{rate}=k[\ce{A}]$, so

$$k=\frac{\text{rate}}{[\ce{A}]}=\frac{\text{mol L}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}}{\text{mol L}^{-1}}=\text{s}^{-1}$$

Because the units cancel, the rate constant of a first-order reaction has the dimension of reciprocal time — this is also why $t_{1/2}=0.693/k$ comes out in units of time.

questions.question: What is the geometry of complex [Ti(H$_2$O)$_6$]$^{3+}$?
questions.answer:
**[Ti(H$_2$O)$_6$]$^{3+}$ is octahedral.**

Ti$^{3+}$ has the configuration $3d^1$ (Ti is $3d^24s^2$, so losing three electrons leaves one d electron). With six ligands the complex is $sp^3d^2$ (outer-orbital) octahedral — a regular octahedron with six water molecules at the corners and Ti at the centre. Its single d electron can be excited between the $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ levels, which is why the ion is **purple-violet** in aqueous solution.

questions.question: Which is the most electronegative element in periodic table?
questions.answer:
**Fluorine** (electronegativity 3.98 on the Pauling scale) — the most electronegative element.

Its very small size and seven valence electrons give it the greatest tendency to attract a shared pair. On the Mulliken scale too it tops the list, and oxygen (3.44) is second. Caesium and francium are the least electronegative.

questions.question: Write the electronic configuration of Co$^{2+}$ (Z = 27).
questions.answer:
Cobalt: $[\ce{Ar}]\,3d^7 4s^2$. Removing the two 4s electrons first gives

$$\ce{Co^{2+}}:\ [\ce{Ar}]\,3d^7$$

or, written in full,

$$1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^6\,3s^2\,3p^6\,3d^7$$

With three unpaired d electrons ($3d^7$: $\uparrow\downarrow\ \uparrow\downarrow\ \uparrow\ \uparrow\ \uparrow$ in a weak field), Co$^{2+}$ is **paramagnetic**, with $\mu=\sqrt{3\times5}=3.87$ B.M., and its salts are coloured.

questions.question: Name two nucleic acids.
questions.answer:
**DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid)** and **RNA (ribonucleic acid)**.

DNA stores the genetic information as a double helix of deoxyribonucleotides (sugar 2-deoxy-D-ribose; bases A, G, C, T). RNA is a single strand of ribonucleotides (sugar D-ribose; uracil in place of thymine) and occurs as mRNA, tRNA and rRNA, carrying out protein synthesis.

questions.question: Write the monomers of Buna-S.
questions.answer:
**1,3-Butadiene** ($\ce{CH2=CH-CH=CH2}$) and **styrene** ($\ce{C6H5CH=CH2}$).

Copolymerising them in the presence of sodium gives Buna-S (styrene–butadiene rubber):

$$\ce{nCH2=CH-CH=CH2 + nC6H5CH=CH2 ->[-Na] [-CH2-CH=CH-CH2-CH(C6H5)-CH2-]_n}$$

It is a tough, abrasion-resistant synthetic rubber used chiefly for tyres.

questions.question: Name any one antacid.
questions.answer:
**Sodium hydrogen carbonate, $\ce{NaHCO3}$** — it neutralises excess hydrochloric acid in the stomach:

$$\ce{NaHCO3 + HCl -> NaCl + H2O + CO2 ^}$$

Another common antacid is **magnesium hydroxide, $\ce{Mg(OH)2}$** (milk of magnesia), often combined with aluminium hydroxide gel. Antacids raise the gastric pH and so relieve the pain of hyperacidity and peptic ulcer.

questions.question: Differentiate between Schottky and Frenkel defect.
questions.answer:
| Schottky defect | Frenkel defect |
|---|---|
| Some ions are **missing** from the lattice — equal numbers of cations and anions leave their sites | An ion leaves its lattice site and occupies an **interstitial** position in the same crystal |
| The crystal stays electrically neutral but its **density decreases** | Mass and volume are unchanged, so **density is unaffected** |
| Found in highly ionic compounds of similar-sized ions with high coordination number: **NaCl, KCl, CsCl, AgBr** | Found where the cation and anion differ greatly in size: **AgCl, AgBr, ZnS** |
| The number of vacancies is equal for both ions | No ions are lost, only displaced |
| Lowers the density; raises ionic conductivity | Does not change density; also raises conductivity and gives colour (e.g. AgBr turns yellow) |

Both are point defects that raise the ionic conductivity of the crystal.

questions.question: The vapour pressure of pure benzene at a certain temperature is 0·850 bar. A non-volatile, non-electrolyte solid weighing 0·5 g is added to 39·0 g of benzene (molar mass 78 g mol$^{-1}$). The vapour pressure of the solution obtained is 0·845 bar. What is the molar mass of the solid substance?
questions.answer:
By Raoult's law the relative lowering of vapour pressure equals the mole fraction of the solute:

$$\frac{p^\circ-p_s}{p^\circ}=\frac{n_2}{n_1+n_2}$$

$$\frac{0.850-0.845}{0.850}=\frac{0.005}{0.850}=5.88\times10^{-3}$$

Moles of benzene:

$$n_1=\frac{39.0}{78}=0.500\ \text{mol}$$

Since $n_2\ll n_1$, the denominator is essentially $n_1$:

$$n_2=5.88\times10^{-3}\times0.500=2.94\times10^{-3}\ \text{mol}$$

(Solving exactly, $n_2=2.96\times10^{-3}$ mol — the dilute approximation is good to 1%.)

$$M_2=\frac{w_2}{n_2}=\frac{0.5}{2.94\times10^{-3}}=170\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$$

**The molar mass of the solid is about 170 g mol$^{-1}$** (169–170 depending on rounding) — consistent with a substance such as anthracene (178) or a simple aromatic compound.

questions.question: What are lyophilic and lyophobic sols? Explain with examples.
questions.answer:
**Lyophilic sols** ('solvent-loving') are colloidal sols in which the dispersed phase has a strong **affinity for the dispersion medium**; the particles are solvated, so the sol is formed easily (simply by warming or shaking the substance with the medium) and is **very stable and reversible** — if the medium is evaporated, the sol reforms on adding more. They are also called **intrinsic colloids** and are largely self-stabilised, needing little or no electrolyte. **Examples: gum in water, starch sol, gelatin, albumin, rubber in benzene.**

**Lyophobic sols** ('solvent-hating') are those in which the dispersed phase has **little or no affinity** for the medium; they cannot be made by simple mixing but need special methods (Bredig's arc, peptization, chemical double decomposition), and they are **less stable and irreversible** — once coagulated, they cannot be reconstituted by adding the medium. They are stabilised only by adsorbed ions, so even a small amount of electrolyte coagulates them. **Examples: sols of metals (gold, silver), $\ce{As2S3}$ sol, ferric hydroxide sol, sulphur sol.**

When water is the medium they are called **hydrosols** (hydrophilic/hydrophobic).

questions.question: Calculate the magnetic moment of: (a) Sc$^{3+}$ (Z = 21) (b) V$^{3+}$ (Z = 23)
questions.answer:
The spin-only magnetic moment is

$$\mu=\sqrt{n(n+2)}\ \text{B.M.}$$

where $n$ is the number of unpaired d electrons.

**(a) Sc$^{3+}$ (Z = 21):** Sc is $[\ce{Ar}]3d^14s^2$, so Sc$^{3+}$ is $[\ce{Ar}]3d^0$ — **no d electrons at all**:

$$n=0\ \Rightarrow\ \mu=0\ \text{B.M.}$$

It is **diamagnetic and colourless**.

**(b) V$^{3+}$ (Z = 23):** V is $[\ce{Ar}]3d^34s^2$, so V$^{3+}$ is $[\ce{Ar}]3d^2$ — two unpaired electrons ($\uparrow\ \uparrow\ \_\ \_\ \_$):

$$\mu=\sqrt{2(2+2)}=\sqrt{8}=2.83\ \text{B.M.}$$

So Sc$^{3+}$ is 0 B.M. (diamagnetic) and V$^{3+}$ is 2.83 B.M. (paramagnetic).

questions.question: Using IUPAC norms write the systematic names of the following: (a) [Co(NH$_3$)$_4$(H$_2$O)$_2$]Cl$_3$ (b) [Co(en)$_3$]$^{3+}$ (c) [NiCl$_4$]$^{2-}$
questions.answer:
**(a) [Co(NH$_3$)$_4$(H$_2$O)$_2$]Cl$_3$** — the cation has a charge of +3, so Co is +3; ligands (four ammine, two aqua) are named alphabetically, ammine before aqua:

**tetraamminediaquacobalt(III) chloride**

**(b) [Co(en)$_3$]$^{3+}$** — three bidentate ethylenediamine ligands around Co(III):

**tris(ethylenediamine)cobalt(III) ion**

(the prefix *tris* is used because the ligand name already contains a prefix-like syllable; the complex is chiral, having $\Delta$ and $\Lambda$ forms).

**(c) [NiCl$_4$]$^{2-}$** — four chlorido ligands, each −1, with Ni: $x+4(-1)=-2\Rightarrow x=+2$:

**tetrachloridonickelate(II) ion**

(The complex is tetrahedral; the -ate ending marks the anionic complex.)

questions.question: Predict the product: (a) phenol $\xrightarrow{CHCl_3/\text{aq. }NaOH}$ (b) benzene + CH$_3$COCl $\xrightarrow{\text{anhyd. }AlCl_3}$ (c) $\ce{CH3CH2CH=CH2 + HBr ->[\text{peroxide}]}$
questions.answer:
**(a) Reimer–Tiemann reaction** — phenol with chloroform and aqueous alkali gives salicylaldehyde (2-hydroxybenzaldehyde), the $\ce{-CHO}$ entering ortho to the OH:

$$\ce{C6H5OH + CHCl3 + 3NaOH ->[\text{hydrolysis}] o-HOC6H4CHO + 3NaCl + 2H2O}$$

The reactive species is dichlorocarbene, $\ce{:CCl2}$, generated from chloroform and hydroxide.

**(b) Friedel-Crafts acylation** — acetophenone:

$$\ce{C6H6 + CH3COCl ->[AlCl3] C6H5COCH3 + HCl}$$

**(c) Free-radical (peroxide-effect) addition** — anti-Markovnikov addition of HBr, so the Br goes to the terminal carbon:

$$\ce{CH3CH2CH=CH2 + HBr ->[\text{peroxide}] CH3CH2CH2CH2Br}$$

**1-Bromobutane** is the product (in the absence of peroxide the Markovnikov product, 2-bromobutane, would form).

questions.question: How will you bring about the following transformations? (a) Benzene to nitrobenzene (b) Ethane nitrile to ethanamine (c) Toluene to benzoic acid.
questions.answer:
**(a) Benzene → nitrobenzene:** nitration with a mixture of concentrated nitric and sulphuric acids at 323–333 K, the electrophile being the nitronium ion $\ce{NO2^+}$:

$$\ce{C6H6 + HNO3 ->[H2SO4][323-333 K] C6H5NO2 + H2O}$$

**(b) Ethanenitrile → ethanamine:** catalytic hydrogenation (or LiAlH$_4$) reduces the nitrile to a primary amine:

$$\ce{CH3CN + 2H2 ->[Ni] CH3CH2NH2}$$

$$\ce{or\ CH3CN + LiAlH4 ->[H2O] CH3CH2NH2}$$

**(c) Toluene → benzoic acid:** the side-chain methyl group is oxidised to carboxyl by boiling with alkaline KMnO$_4$, then acidifying:

$$\ce{C6H5CH3 ->[KMnO4][KOH,\ \Delta] C6H5COOK ->[H3O^+] C6H5COOH}$$

Hot acidified dichromate works equally well.

questions.question: The rate of a particular reaction doubles when temperature changes from 27°C to 37°C. Calculate the energy of activation of such a reaction. (Given log 2 = 0·30)
questions.answer:
Use the two-temperature form of the Arrhenius equation:

$$\log\frac{k_2}{k_1}=\frac{E_a}{2.303R}\left(\frac{T_2-T_1}{T_1T_2}\right)$$

Given $k_2/k_1=2$, $T_1=300$ K, $T_2=310$ K, $R=8.314$ J K$^{-1}$ mol$^{-1}$:

$$\log2=\frac{E_a}{2.303\times8.314}\times\frac{310-300}{300\times310}$$

$$0.30=\frac{E_a}{19.147}\times\frac{10}{93000}=\frac{E_a}{19.147}\times1.0753\times10^{-4}$$

$$E_a=\frac{0.30\times19.147}{1.0753\times10^{-4}}$$

$$E_a=5.344\times10^{4}\ \text{J mol}^{-1}=53.4\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$$

**The energy of activation is about 53.4 kJ mol$^{-1}$.**

This is the familiar 'rate doubles for a 10 K rise' rule: substituting $E_a$ back shows that near room temperature a 10 K increase roughly doubles $k$ for reactions with $E_a\approx50$–55 kJ mol$^{-1}$. A large activation energy makes the rate much more temperature-sensitive.

questions.question: Write the required conditions to maximise the yield of ammonia by Haber's process. What happens when NH$_3$ reacts with (a) Cu$^{2+}$ and (b) Cl$_2$?
questions.answer:
**The reaction:**

$$\ce{N2(g) + 3H2(g) <=> 2NH3(g)},\qquad \Delta H=-92.4\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$$

It is reversible, **exothermic**, and accompanied by a **decrease in volume** (4 mol of gas → 2 mol).

**Conditions for maximum yield (Le Chatelier's principle):**

1. **Low temperature** — the forward reaction is exothermic, so a low temperature shifts the equilibrium to the right. In practice a compromise of about **723–773 K (≈700 K)** is used, because below this the rate becomes too slow even with a catalyst.
2. **High pressure** — four volumes of gas become two, so compression favours ammonia. About **200 atm** (200×10$^5$ Pa) is used, limited by the strength of the vessels and the cost of compression.
3. **Catalyst** — finely divided **iron with promoters** (K$_2$O, Al$_2$O$_3$, CaO) to reach equilibrium quickly without changing the position of equilibrium.
4. Removal of ammonia by **liquefaction** and recycling of the unreacted N$_2$ + H$_2$ drives the reaction further forward.

**(a) With Cu$^{2+}$:** ammonia acts as a ligand and gives a deep blue complex (this is the test for Cu$^{2+}$):

$$\ce{Cu^{2+} + 4NH3 -> [Cu(NH3)4]^{2+}}\quad(\text{deep blue})$$

**(b) With Cl$_2$:** ammonia reduces chlorine; with excess chlorine nitrogen is liberated, and with excess ammonia the chloramine is formed instead:

$$\ce{8NH3 + 3Cl2 -> N2 + 6NH4Cl}$$

With **excess ammonia** chloramine is formed instead:

$$\ce{2NH3 + Cl2 -> NH2Cl + NH4Cl}$$

The first reaction is used to detect a chlorine leak in cylinders (white fumes of NH$_4$Cl).

questions.question: Draw the structures of the following compounds: (a) N$_2$O$_5$ (b) H$_3$PO$_3$ (c) H$_4$P$_2$O$_7$ (d) H$_2$SO$_4$ (e) XeOF$_2$
questions.answer:
**(a) $\ce{N2O5}$** — planear, $\ce{O2N-O-NO2}$: each N is bonded to two oxygens by double bonds and the two halves are joined by a single N–O–N bridge (angle ≈130°). In the solid state it is the salt $\ce{[NO2]^+[NO3]^-}$.

**(b) $\ce{H3PO3}$** — phosphorus(III) tetrahedral: one $\ce{P=O}$, **two P–OH** and **one P–H**, written $\ce{O=P(H)(OH)2}$. The P–H hydrogen is not acidic, so the acid is **dibasic**.

**(c) $\ce{H4P2O7}$** (pyrophosphoric acid) — two PO$_4$ tetrahedra sharing one oxygen: $\ce{(HO)2P(O)-O-P(O)(OH)2}$, i.e. each P carries one $\ce{P=O}$ and two $\ce{-OH}$ groups, the two tetrahedra being joined by a bridging $\ce{-O-}$. With four ionisable $\ce{-OH}$ protons it is **tetrabasic**.

**(d) $\ce{H2SO4}$** — sulphur(VI) tetrahedral: two $\ce{S=O}$ double bonds and two $\ce{S-OH}$ single bonds, i.e. $\ce{HO-SO2-OH}$; dibasic.

**(e) $\ce{XeOF2}$** — xenon(IV), $sp^3d$; **T-shaped**: two F and one O (as $\ce{Xe=O}$) around Xe, with two lone pairs occupying the remaining trigonal-bipyramidal positions.

questions.question: Write short notes on the following: (a) Aldol condensation (b) Williamson's synthesis (c) Carbylamine reaction.
questions.answer:
**(a) Aldol condensation.** Aldehydes or ketones having at least one **$\alpha$-hydrogen** condense with one another in the presence of dilute alkali to give a $\beta$-hydroxy aldehyde or ketone — an 'aldol' — which loses water on heating to give an $\alpha$,$\beta$-unsaturated carbonyl compound:

$$\ce{CH3CHO + CH3CHO ->[dil. NaOH] CH3CH(OH)CH2CHO ->[\Delta] CH3CH=CHCHO + H2O}$$

The base removes the acidic $\alpha$-H to form a carbanion, which attacks the carbonyl carbon of the second molecule. With propanone the product is diacetone alcohol.

**(b) Williamson's synthesis.** This is the standard laboratory method for **ethers**: a sodium alkoxide is treated with a primary alkyl halide, and S$_N$2 displacement gives the ether:

$$\ce{R-ONa + R'-X -> R-O-R' + NaX}$$

$$\ce{C2H5ONa + C2H5Br -> C2H5-O-C2H5 + NaBr}$$

It works best with **primary** halides; tertiary halides eliminate instead. It can be used for unsymmetrical ethers and for aryl alkyl ethers (e.g. anisole from sodium phenoxide and methyl iodide).

**(c) Carbylamine reaction.** **Primary** amines — aliphatic or aromatic — on warming with chloroform and alcoholic KOH give the foul-smelling **isocyanide**:

$$\ce{RNH2 + CHCl3 + 3KOH ->[\Delta] RNC + 3KCl + 3H2O}$$

$$\ce{C2H5NH2 + CHCl3 + 3KOH -> C2H5NC + 3KCl + 3H2O}$$

It is the standard **test for a primary amine**: secondary and tertiary amines give no isocyanide, and the unbearable smell is unmistakable.

questions.question: Identify 'A', 'B', 'C', 'D' and 'E' in the following: (a) $\ce{CH2=CH2 ->[Br2/H2O] A ->[KOH(aq)] B}$ (b) $\ce{CH3CH(Br)CH3 ->[KOH(alc)] C ->[HBr][\mathrm{peroxide}] D}$ (c) acetophenone $\xrightarrow[\mathrm{heat}]{conc.\ H2SO4}$ E
questions.answer:
**(a)** Ethene with bromine water gives the **bromohydrin** (2-bromoethanol); aqueous KOH then replaces the bromine by OH to give **ethylene glycol**:

$$\ce{CH2=CH2 + Br2/H2O -> CH2Br-CH2OH (A)}$$

$$\ce{CH2Br-CH2OH ->[KOH(aq)][\Delta] HOCH2-CH2OH (B)}$$

(An intramolecular route through oxirane is involved, which ring-opens to the glycol.) So **A = 2-bromoethanol, B = ethane-1,2-diol**.

**(b)** Alcoholic KOH eliminates HBr to give **propene (C)**; with peroxide, HBr adds anti-Markovnikov to give **1-bromopropane (D)**:

$$\ce{CH3CH(Br)CH3 ->[KOH(alc)] CH3CH=CH2 (C) ->[HBr/\text{peroxide}] CH3CH2CH2Br (D)}$$

**(c)** Acetophenone, $\ce{C6H5COCH3}$, heated with concentrated sulphuric acid, undergoes acid-catalysed self-condensation (an aldol-type condensation followed by dehydration and cyclisation), and **three molecules combine to give 1,3,5-triphenylbenzene (E)** — the aromatic analogue of the way acetone gives mesitylene:

$$\ce{3C6H5COCH3 ->[conc. H2SO4][\Delta] 1,3,5-C6H3(C6H5)3 + 3H2O}$$

**Summary: A = 2-bromoethanol, B = ethane-1,2-diol, C = propene, D = 1-bromopropane, E = 1,3,5-triphenylbenzene.**
